title: Tesla (TSLA) Stock Gets Fair Value Bump As Analysts Split On AI And SpaceX
detail:
Tesla (TSLA) Stock Gets Fair Value Bump As Analysts Split On AI And SpaceX
Bailey Pemberton
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 11:09 AM PDT 4 min read
TSLA
SPCX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Tesla's analyst fair value estimate has shifted from US$395.57 to US$408.36, giving investors a fresh reference point for where some models place the stock. Much of this recalibration links back to the split in analyst views, with bullish perspectives tying higher targets to AI, autonomy and the possible SpaceX merger. More cautious perspectives flag cash burn, heavy capex and execution risk around Robotaxi, Cybercab, Optimus, Semi and Roadster. As you read on, you will see how these moving targets shape the Tesla story and what to watch as the narrative keeps evolving.

Stay updated as the Fair Value for Tesla shifts by adding it to your watchlist or portfolio. Alternatively, explore our Community to discover new perspectives on Tesla.

What Wall Street Has Been Saying
🐂 Bullish Takeaways

Cantor Fitzgerald, Piper Sandler, Mizuho and Tigress Financial highlight Tesla's Q3 report, margin profile and expanding FSD, Robotaxi, Cybercab and Optimus efforts as supportive of higher price targets in the US$460 to US$550 range and ongoing AI led growth optionality.

Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan and Stifel point to improving auto and energy fundamentals, stronger than expected automotive gross margins in Q3 and progress on Robotaxi scaling and FSD adoption as factors that reinforce their Neutral or Buy stances with targets around US$400 to US$415 and an adjusted US$491 target at Stifel.

RBC Capital, CLSA, Barclays and BNP Paribas flag the potential Tesla and SpaceX merger as a key part of the bull case, with targets such as US$400 at CLSA, US$420 at BNP Paribas and a reduced but still high US$480 at RBC that frame the combined AI, connectivity and robotics story as an important valuation support.

🐻 Bearish Takeaways

BNP Paribas, JPMorgan and Jefferies keep a cautious tone around Tesla's multi year cash burn, higher spending and lower margin assumptions, even as they raise or trim targets into the US$400 to US$420 range and move ratings only to Neutral or Hold.

Phillip Securities and Wells Fargo focus on pressure from heavy capex and product execution. Phillip Securities raises its target to US$230 but maintains a Sell rating after Q3 spending absorbed margin gains, while Wells Fargo views the Cybercab launch as underwhelming versus expectations and keeps an Underweight rating with a US$130 target.

Tesla Stock Is Down 17% Over the Past Year. Buy Now or Wait for Merger Terms?
Gian Estrada

Trading disclosure
Tesla Stock Is Down 17% Over the Past Year. Buy Now or Wait for Merger Terms? ©@inkdrop via Canva, @Matt Weissinger from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Tesla stock is down 17.1% over the past year, closing at $372.22 on October 23, with the worst damage coming after a second-quarter report that showed a $1.1B cash burn.

The Street's mean target of $408.36 sits 9.7% above the close.

Q3 free cash flow swung back to $1.53B as Tesla cut its 2026 capex guide to about $20B from more than $25B.

SpaceX says any Tesla merger would need approval from Musk as its controlling shareholder, and no terms exist yet.

Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) stock is down 17.1% over the past year, closing at $372.22 on October 23, after a July report that paired Tesla's first cash burn in more than two years with a spending plan of more than $25 billion.

The October report undid part of that. Free cash flow swung back to positive and Tesla cut its spending guide, yet the shares fell 2% the next day. Tesla stock now sits 16.4% above its July 23 close of $319.69 and 25.4% below its record intraday high (by my math).

Tesla Stock Peaked in December, Then Spent Spring Giving It Back
TSLA Stock Price: 1-Year (TIKR)

The one-year window opens at $449.00, working back from the printed return. Tesla stock hit a record intraday high of $498.83 in December, and spent the next four months sliding: it closed 2025 at $450 and ended March at $372.

The first-quarter delivery count didn't help. On April 2, Tesla reported 358,023 deliveries against a Visible Alpha estimate of 368,903, and the stock bottomed in the mid-$340s that month.

A rally into the mid-$440s followed in May with no single event behind it. By June 30 the stock closed at $421, and on July 2 Tesla delivered 480,126 vehicles, 19.2% above the 402,776 the Street expected. That beat lasted three weeks.

The July 22 Report That Did the Real Damage

Tesla's second quarter looked fine at the top line: revenue of $28.24 billion against a $25.71 billion estimate. Below it, things fell apart. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.33 against the $0.51 analysts expected, and operating margin shrank to 1.4%.

The bigger problem was capital expenditure (capex, the money spent on factories, chips and equipment). Tesla spent $5.8 billion in the quarter, pushing free cash flow to negative $1.1 billion. CFO Vaibhav Taneja kept the 2026 capex guide above $25 billion, said spending would grow for the next two or three years, and warned that negative free cash flow would deepen in the second half.

Tesla stock fell 14.5% to $319.69 on July 23, its biggest drop since March 2025, according to Bloomberg. That's 24.1% below the June 30 close in less than four weeks, and the slide carried the stock near $300 in early August.

title: Tesla stock sellers should pump their brakes, 5-star analyst says
detail:
Tesla stock sellers should pump their brakes, 5-star analyst says
Tony Owusu, Aparajita Chatterjee
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 6:33 AM PDT 4 min read
TSLA
Trade Tesla on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Despite surprise top- and bottom-line beats, Tesla shares took a bit of a haircut this week immediately following the release of its third-quarter results. Investors who dug beneath the surface seemingly weren't that impressed with the 48 cents per share in profit (vs. 43 cents exp.) and $28.05 billion (vs. $27.9 billion exp.) that the electric vehicle maker reported for the period.

That may be because the further you dig, you find that revenue was slightly down year over year, as core automotive revenue declined 3% and energy revenue fell 16%. Tesla blamed the decrease in automotive revenue on lower average sale prices for its cars and trouble securing battery supplies to make enough vehicles to fulfill backlog orders.

Also read: Elon Musk wants every American kid to own a SpaceX share

But despite the mixed results, analysts at Morgan Stanley say they are incrementally more constructive on Tesla thanks to the bigger picture: Robotaxi scaling and Full Self-Driving (Supervised) adoption.

Tesla Robotaxi strategy is working, Morgan Stanley says

Earlier this year, CEO Elon Musk announced that the company was raising its capital expenditure guidance for 2026 to $25 billion in order to scale up Tesla's Robotaxi and humanoid robot operations (however, Tesla did lower its Capex guidance back down to more than $20 billion in the quarter, so it is unclear how that will affect expansion plans).

About nine months later, Morgan Stanley analyst Andrew Percoco is starting to see the results.

"Tesla's results reinforce our view that the company is making tangible progress toward commercializing autonomy and robotics, with encouraging proof points around FSD adoption and Robotaxi fleet growth," Percoco said in a note this week that was viewed by TheStreet.

"We view this acceleration as an encouraging indication that Tesla is beginning to move beyond the initial software validation phase toward more meaningful commercial scaling."

title: Good News for Tesla Investors: 3 Key Benchmarks Elon Musk's Company Delivered On in the Third Quarter
detail:
Good News for Tesla Investors: 3 Key Benchmarks Elon Musk's Company Delivered On in the Third Quarter
Lee Samaha, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 4:10 AM PDT 5 min read
TSLA
NVDA
SPCX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Although Tesla's (NASDAQ: TSLA) earnings call certainly wasn't as polished as the Space Exploration Technologies one the previous day, it was no less compelling. The company met three key benchmarks many investors were looking for in Tesla, and investors have reason to feel more positive about the stock as a result. Here's why.

Tesla's earnings: Substance over presentation

The key to the medium-term investment case for Tesla is its Robotaxi rollout, how it can finance it (and its other investments, such as Optimus), and whether it retains its leadership position in electric vehicles (EVs) to continue self-funding its development. All three issues were addressed, directly or indirectly, in the benchmarks and numbers from the company's third-quarter earnings report and presentation.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Automotive gross margin recovery

Gross margins matter because they are key indicators of a company's pricing power, competitiveness, and ability to generate future earnings growth and cash flow. Going back to the second quarter, Tesla reported a big increase in sequential automotive sales (from $15.5 billion in the first quarter to $20 billion in the second quarter). Still, the market was concerned by the drop in sequential gross profit margin (excluding regulatory credit sales) from 19.2% to 16.3%.

The key question going into the third quarter was whether the number would recover or a further decline would signal a loss of Tesla's competitiveness as it was forced to offer financial incentives to boost sales. The answer is in the chart, with a sequential improvement to 18.3% signaling strong demand. This was confirmed on the earnings call, with Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk noting, "Demand is growing rapidly for our vehicles. It's exceeding our production by a significant margin."

With global vehicle inventories down to just 11 days from 27 days at the end of the first quarter, it's unlikely Tesla needs to offer significant financial incentives now.

Data source: Tesla presentations. Chart by the author.
Tesla eases cash flow concerns

Let's face facts: The Robotaxi rollout has been much slower than Musk estimated last year. As such, cash flow projections for Tesla from recurring robotaxi earnings have been pushed out.

At the same time, management has raised expectations for up-front capital expenditure (capex) this year, forecasting full-year capex of more than $20 billion in January, then more than $25 billion in April, and again in June. However, Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja dialed back expectations to "approximately $20 billion for the current year as a result of managing our capital deployment efficiently."

title: Elon Musk Wants to Give Every American Child a Share of SpaceX. Here's What It Would Cost -- and What It Means for Everyone Else Holding the Stock
detail:
Elon Musk Wants to Give Every American Child a Share of SpaceX. Here's What It Would Cost -- and What It Means for Everyone Else Holding the Stock
James Brumley, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 2:07 AM PDT 4 min read
SPCX
TSLA
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Elon Musk just promised millions of people a gift. On Monday, the co-founder and CEO of Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) and Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) wrote in a post at X -- the social media platform formerly known as Twitter -- "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America." He then added, "This will be the first of many."

It sounds good, particularly if you're one of those children about to receive the gift. But what will it cost, and who pays other than Musk?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Musk didn't add any other details. We can, however, make some reasonable assumptions about how this will work.

More than enough already in hand

Musk doesn't need to dilute existing shareholders by issuing new shares of SPCX to make good on his gift. Musk himself effectively controls or personally owns 6.4 billion A shares of the recently public company, in addition to 3.9 billion B shares. There's another 1.3 billion restricted B shares that could soon become his as well, plus 350 million more that he could purchase if he chooses to exercise his options.

For comparison, there are currently just over 72 million children under the age of 18 residing in the United States, according to The Annie E. Casey Foundation. Assuming Musk is using the same standard about who qualifies as a kid, he could give away a mere 1.8% of the 3.9 billion B shares he already owns and still fulfill his promise.

SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk. Image source: The White House.

His total net cost? At today's price, that's roughly $12 billion worth of SPCX stock, which, of course, is only a fraction of his estimated net worth of right around $1 trillion right now.

And it's almost certainly SpaceX's B shares that Musk intends to give away. Although he personally owns just a little less than half of the company, the A shares' voting power is 10 times that of B shares, effectively giving Musk 85% control of Space Exploration Technologies. He's not apt to give any of that up.

Barely a blip

As for what it means to every other SPCX shareholder, the answer is not a lot... at least not initially. Musk can personally afford to fund the entirety of this gift. No dilution is necessary.

Longer-term, though, there is a slight conceivable impact. This will put a single share of SpaceX stock in 72 million different investors' hands, with little clarity as to how or even whether selling it will be restricted. Hopefully, most of these recipients will hang onto it indefinitely and use it as a seed for a retirement nest egg. Many of them will likely sell it at their first opportunity, however.

Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) and General Motors (NYSE: GM) may seem light-years apart in how Wall Street views each automaker, but both are interesting stocks given what they can offer investors. If I had to choose just one to buy today, the answer isn't necessarily obvious. Let's have a deeper look.

GM is buying back shares

GM doesn't grab headlines like Tesla, but the legacy car and truck manufacturer is posting numbers that should attract buy-and-hold investors. On Oct. 20, GM released its third-quarter results, which showed revenue of $50 billion, a nearly 3% increase from last year. The company also approved a new $20 billion share buyback and increased its full-year guidance for adjusted automotive free cash flow to $11.5 billion to $12.5 billion.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Wall Street wasn't overly impressed with GM's results. It instead focused on potential cost increases due to inflation and lingering electric-vehicle losses. I believe these fears are largely overblown, and there was more positive news for GM than negative with this report.

Image source: Getty Images.
Tesla's future is promising, but pricey

Tesla trades at a premium, but that's because Wall Street has high expectations for Elon Musk's company. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in its latest quarter, beating analysts' expectations but down more than 2% from last year.

Investors in Tesla aren't paying for just EVs. They're investing in Tesla's robotaxis, Optimus, and full self-driving capabilities. It's a far more complicated and multifaceted manufacturer than GM or other legacy automakers.

Even with Tesla's falling net income, the stock is still trading at an incredible premium. Tesla's trailing price-to-earnings ratio is about 351, while its market cap is currently $1.5 trillion. Tesla is priced for perfection. An investment now could pay off, but there are real execution risks. There's also a lot of talk about Tesla potentially merging with Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) in the near future, which adds another layer of uncertainty to the stock.

If I had to choose today, I'd pick GM as the stock to buy. There's more risk and potential upside with Tesla, but GM is consistently profitable, buying back shares, and trading at a very reasonable price.

title: Bank of America resets Tesla forecast as Robotaxi miles double
detail:
Bank of America resets Tesla forecast as Robotaxi miles double
Tobi Opeyemi Amure, Celine Provini
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 6:03 PM PDT 6 min read
TSLA
Trade Tesla on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

For years, Tesla's robotaxi story has been easy to describe and hard to measure.

Elon Musk made promises, Wall Street argued about them, and the actual number of driverless miles stayed small enough to ignore. In July, Tesla's unsupervised fleet had logged about 380,000 miles in total.

That changed over the summer. Tesla now has a growth curve it can point to, and one of Wall Street's bigger Tesla bulls says the curve just bent upward.

If you own Tesla, or an index fund where it ranks among the biggest holdings, this is the number the stock now trades on. Car sales still pay the bills, but the Robotaxi is what investors are paying for.

That makes the pace of growth, not just the promise, the thing worth watching. A service that adds a few thousand miles a month is a science project. One that doubles every few weeks starts to look like a business.

However, a less flattering detail sits a few pages deeper in the same research.

Tesla's (TSLA) Robotaxi service "has hit an inflection point," Bank of America analyst Alexander Perry wrote in an Oct. 22 research note reviewed by TheStreet.

He kept a Buy rating and a $460 price objective, about 19% above the $386.47 price the bank used, while trimming his 2027 earnings estimate to $2.26 a share from $2.47.

Tesla's Robotaxi miles doubled in about four weeks

The bank's math is simple. Unsupervised miles grew from 380,000 on July 22 to 1 million on Sept. 3, then to roughly 2 million by Sept. 30, Perry wrote.

Weekly growth sped up from 17% to about 20% after Tesla added the two-seat Cybercab to its Austin fleet, the note said. Cybercabs now make up 45% of the Texas fleet, according to the bank.

Tesla's own executives described the same surge on the Oct. 21 earnings call. "Accumulative unsupervised miles 8x in the quarter, as we had weekly double-digit growth throughout the quarter," said Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja.

Related: Tesla Robotaxi prices just jumped. Here is what riders pay now

Production is no longer the bottleneck, Tesla says. "Right now, we're building at the rate that the Robotaxi service needs the vehicles," said Lars Moravy, Tesla's vice president of vehicle engineering.

Perry credited the software. "We believe TSLA's comfort in scaling its robotaxi service more rapidly is being enabled by running on a more advanced version of FSD [Full Self-Driving] compared to the consumer fleet," he wrote.

Bank of America says Tesla's unsupervised Robotaxi miles doubled in about four weeks, calling it an "inflection point."Bloomberg / Getty Images
Why Tesla's base business still matters

Under the Robotaxi story, Tesla's quarter was mixed. Revenue was flat at $28.05 billion, while adjusted earnings of 48 cents a share beat estimates, Electrek reported.

title: Musk Calls Tesla’s Merger Vote “Quite a High Hurdle.” JPMorgan’s Premium Math Puts the Stock Near $500.
detail:
Musk Calls Tesla’s Merger Vote “Quite a High Hurdle.” JPMorgan’s Premium Math Puts the Stock Near $500.
Roxanna Maglangit
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 8:33 AM PDT 5 min read
TSLA
SPCX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Musk Calls Tesla's Merger Vote "Quite a High Hurdle." JPMorgan's Premium Math Puts the Stock Near $500. ©U.S. Air Force photo by Trevor Cokley and kb group via Canva

[IMAGE CREDIT: U.S. Air Force photo by Trevor Cokley and kb group via Canva]

Key Takeaways

Elon Musk said on SpaceX's Oct. 20 earnings call that a SpaceX-Tesla merger would need the votes of 50% of all Tesla shares, and that the two companies' special committees haven't agreed on terms.

JPMorgan expects a SpaceX-led all-stock deal at a typical 30% to 35% premium, which works out to about $486 to $505 a share on Tesla's $373.71 close.

If turnout matches the roughly 74% at Tesla's 2025 annual meeting, a deal would need about two-thirds of the votes cast.

Tesla's new auto-vote program for retail holders could narrow that gap, but it's brand new and no enrollment figures are public.

A lot of Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) investors treat a merger with SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) as a done deal. Elon Musk isn't one of them.

Deutsche Bank's Edison Yu asked about a merger on SpaceX's earnings call Tuesday. Musk started with: "I feel like I'm tap dancing through a mine field."

Musk said both companies have set up special committees of independent directors, and he stays out of their talks as a conflicted party. He thinks a deal would be a good idea. Then he named the problem:

"particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50% vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that's quite a high hurdle to try to achieve."

Wall Street has mostly skipped over that part.

JPMorgan expects a SpaceX-led all-stock deal at a typical 30% to 35% premium to Tesla's current valuation, a structure that would keep Musk in majority voting control of the combined company. On Tesla's $373.71 close Tuesday, that's about $486 to $505 a share.

TIKR tracks 44 analysts on Tesla. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Tesla, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Tesla's Analyst Ratings

Every missing ballot counts as a no

Tesla needs a majority of all its shares, so any share that doesn't vote works against the deal.

And plenty of Tesla shares don't vote. Turnout at its 2025 annual meeting was about 74%, one of its best rates yet. At that turnout, a merger would need about 68% of the votes cast just to reach half of all shares.

Tesla has already seen how this plays out. In 2025, its proposal to drop its supermajority voting rules won about 54% of the shares that voted. That came to only 39.4% of all shares.

Barclays put broker non-votes at about 11% of Tesla's outstanding votes at that meeting. In its request to the SEC, Tesla cited Broadridge data showing that retail investors voted only 28% of their shares in the 2025 proxy season, against 76.6% for institutions. And few stocks have a retail following like Tesla's.
